title: Large-scale Uncertainty Quantification for Latent Variable Models Using Subsampling Markov Chain Monte Carlo
one_liner: Analyze noisy Langevin updates and intermittent Gibbs refreshes together, then tune their step sizes and refresh rates so the resulting uncertainty estimates track a valid large-sample limit.
lead: Models with hidden variables contain global parameters, which are shared numbers affecting all data points, and local hidden variables attached to individual observations. SGLD-Gibbs scales approximate Bayesian updating to large data by updating global parameters with noisy derivative-based steps and updating only some local variables through Gibbs sampling, which means drawing directly from a conditional probability law. It is fast, but it is hard to know whether its uncertainty estimates are trustworthy because step sizes, batch sizes, and local-refresh schedules interact in complicated ways. This paper studies the joint scaling limit of those interacting updates and converts that limit into tuning guidance.

problem.h2: Fast approximate Bayesian updates do not automatically give valid uncertainty
paras: In a model with hidden variables, global parameters govern the whole population while local hidden variables explain individual examples. Exact Markov chain Monte Carlo is often too slow because every iteration may require touching every local variable.

SGLD-Gibbs cuts that cost by using random mini-batch derivatives for the global parameters and by refreshing only subsets of local variables. That is computationally attractive, but the resulting chain is not an obvious approximation of any simple target. If hyperparameters are set poorly, the method can return narrow or distorted uncertainty intervals even when point estimates look reasonable.

The paper asks a calibration question: under what scaling of step size, time, and local refresh rate does the algorithm converge to a limit that still reflects the uncertainty carried by both global and local randomness after conditioning on the data?

callout.html: Study the joint large-sample limit of noisy global updates and sporadic local updates, then choose algorithm settings that keep that limit faithful to uncertainty after conditioning on the observed data.

panels.title: 1. Global and local unknowns interact
panels.caption: Global parameters depend on many local hidden-state assignments, and vice versa.

panels.title: 2. Large data force subsampling
panels.viz_args: Use mini-batches for gradients and update only some local variables each iteration.
panels.caption: The algorithm must approximate full Bayesian updates to stay scalable.

panels.title: 3. Global parameters move diffusively
panels.caption: Noisy derivative-based steps accumulate into a diffusion-type limit.

panels.title: 4. Local variables jump intermittently
panels.caption: Each local hidden variable changes only when its Gibbs update is selected.

panels.title: 5. Tune the interaction, not each part alone
panels.viz_args: Step size, batch noise, and refresh rate must match the joint limit.
panels.caption: Trustworthy uncertainty appears only when both update mechanisms are scaled compatibly.

steps.b: Subsample data for a random mini-batch derivative
steps.text: Estimate the global-parameter update from a mini-batch instead of the full dataset.
Move the global parameters using the noisy derivative estimate plus injected Gaussian noise.
Select a subset of hidden-state assignments and resample them from their conditional probability laws.
Treat the global path and each local refresh path together under large-sample rescaling.
Set step size and refresh frequency so the stationary behavior matches the desired uncertainty regime.

paras: The paper changes how SGLD-Gibbs is tuned. Instead of picking step sizes and update rates heuristically, it derives them from a limit theorem describing the joint behavior of global and local updates.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: latent-refresh noise contribution
hidden.name: latent-refresh noise contribution
paras: The uncertainty of the global parameters does not come only from derivative-estimate noise. It also comes from randomness in the local latent variables, which are updated intermittently. That contribution is hidden because the global-parameter path only feels it indirectly through changing sufficient statistics and conditional expectations.

The paper makes this contribution explicit by showing that individual local variables converge to jump processes in the scaling limit. Those jumps feed into the effective stationary probability law of the global parameters. Once that interaction is visible, one can tune the algorithm so local-refresh noise is neither ignored nor exaggerated.

heat.caption: Darker cells indicate sources that strongly shape the stationary uncertainty of the global parameters.

reads.html: If local latent variables are refreshed too rarely, the global parameters see stale information and their uncertainty is understated. If local variables are refreshed on the right scale, their randomness enters the global uncertainty correctly.

The scaling limit separates a diffusion-type component for the global parameters from jump-process components for individual latent variables, then identifies how the jump contributions enter the effective stationary law used for uncertainty quantification.

mechanism.h2: Why the jump-diffusion limit gives tuning guidance
paras: A tuning rule is useful only if it connects algorithm settings to the stationary uncertainty eventually produced by the chain. The limit theorem provides exactly that connection. It says that after appropriate rescaling, the global parameters behave as a diffusion, which is a continuous random motion with drift and variance, while local hidden variables behave like jump processes because they only move at refresh times.

That decomposition matters because different hyperparameters control different pieces. The global step size and mini-batch scale control diffusion variance and bias. The local refresh schedule controls how much latent-state randomness is injected into the global dynamics. When the schedule is too slow, the diffusion part is driven by stale conditional structure. When it is too fast relative to the step size, computation is wasted and the approximation enters a different regime than intended.

By identifying the joint limit, the paper can state scaling relations under which the stationary spread of global parameters reflects the right balance of derivative-estimate noise and latent-update noise. That is why the tuning guidance targets uncertainty quality directly rather than only optimization speed.

stages.s: Mini-batch data, current global parameters, and current local latent variables
Update global parameters with a noisy Langevin step based on a mini-batch derivative
Refresh selected local variables by conditional sampling
View the coupled process under large-sample rescaling
Read off the diffusion variance and jump contribution
Hyperparameter rules tied to stationary uncertainty

math.words: The global parameters converge to a diffusion-type limit, while each local latent variable converges to a jump process whose refresh intensity depends on the Gibbs-update schedule. Tuning is chosen so both pieces contribute on the intended scale.
math.equation: global_limit = drift_term + diffusion_noise + latent_jump_contribution, while local_limit is a jump process with refresh intensity r
symbols: average pull of the posterior toward high-probability global-parameter values
random fluctuation induced by mini-batch derivative noise and injected Langevin noise
extra fluctuation transmitted from intermittently updated latent variables
refresh intensity controlling how often local variables jump in the limit

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the global step size is small, but local variables are refreshed only once every many iterations.
Then the diffusion part of the global update is driven by conditional summaries that stay stale for long stretches.
In the scaling limit, the local jump intensity is too low, so latent uncertainty barely enters the stationary spread of the global parameters.
Now increase the refresh rate while keeping the step size on the matched scale suggested by the theory.
The local jump contribution becomes visible in the global limit, and credible intervals for global parameters widen toward the correct uncertainty level.

math.note: The theorem is not only descriptive. It tells which algorithm settings place the approximation in a regime where uncertainty from local latent variables is still represented in the global stationary law.

charts.title: Untuned SGLD-Gibbs
charts.note: The method scales well, but uncertainty can be distorted because step sizes and latent refreshes are chosen without reference to the joint limit.

charts.title: SGLD-Gibbs with scaling guidance
charts.note: Calibration improves because the tuning keeps latent-update randomness on the right scale relative to the noisy global dynamics.

items.b: Finite-sample behavior may differ from the limit.
items.html: The scaling theory describes large-sample behavior. On moderate datasets, the asymptotic regime may not be fully active, so the recommended tuning can still need adjustment based on observed calibration error.

items.b: Conditional Gibbs updates can be expensive or approximate.
items.html: The tuning guidance assumes that local refreshes follow the intended conditional law. If those refreshes are themselves approximated poorly, the jump contribution identified by the theory is misrepresented.

items.b: Model misspecification can hide calibration gains.
items.html: Even with correct scaling, uncertainty from the algorithm reflects the assumed latent variable model. If that model is badly wrong, credible intervals can remain misleading because they are calibrated to the wrong statistical structure.

The guidance is most useful when the latent conditional updates are trustworthy, the data are large enough for the scaling regime to be relevant, and calibration is evaluated against held-out uncertainty targets rather than only point estimates.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Use a model with hidden variables such as a topic model or mixture model with many local assignments. Run SGLD-Gibbs under several step-size and local-refresh schedules, including one schedule matched to the paper's scaling guidance. Measure parameter root-mean-square error, observed coverage of credible intervals for a few global parameters, and runtime per effective sample. The theory-guided schedule should produce interval coverage closer to nominal because the local-refresh randomness enters the global chain on the intended scale.
demo.closing: The demo should show that scalable approximate Bayesian updating is not only about reaching a good point estimate. The interaction between global diffusion noise and local jump noise determines whether the reported uncertainty is believable.
